subtype: Approach: working backward from the target employer [Thinking]
passage:
Francis: ok I looked at the last 10 job posts from the 3 firms I want
Francis: they keep saying "built and deployed", "worked with real data", "owns a feature end to end"
Chaitanya: so not "made a calculator" 😅
Francis: exactly. So my plan: 2 projects. One that cleans and analyses messy data, one that's live on the internet with a real link
Chaitanya: What about the other 8 you were going to do?
Francis: Dropping them. Recruiters won't open ten. I would rather they open two and stay
Chaitanya: Which first?
Francis: The data one. I have the bus-timings data already. 3 weeks
Chaitanya: Send me the link when it's up 🙂

qa.q: How many projects did Francis decide to build?
qa.a: Francis decided to build 2 projects.

qa.q: What is Francis feeling about dropping the other eight projects?
qa.a: Francis feels focused and relieved, saying it is better to have two that recruiters open than ten they skip.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Francis add, and why?
qa.a: Francis could ask a recruiter or an alumnus at those firms what impresses them, because job posts show wording but a person can say what actually gets a project opened.

qa.q: How does Chaitanya see Francis's plan?
qa.a: Chaitanya jokes about calculators, asks what happens to the other eight and asks for the link, so Chaitanya seems supportive and curious.

grounding: Shows planning a portfolio backward from what target employers ask to see, choosing a few substantial projects.

subtype: Approach: storyboarding the portfolio site on paper [Action]
passage:
Monday. Saurabh spread three sheets on the floor of his room and drew the site by hand: a home page with his name and one line about what he builds, three project pages, a contact block. On each project page he drew four boxes and labelled them: problem, my part, result, link.
Wednesday. He showed the sketches to Gurleen, who circled the "result" box on the first project. "This one is empty," she said. "Then I need a real number," Saurabh replied, and wrote himself a note.
Saturday. He opened the editor. Because every page already had its shape, he finished the home page and the first project page before dinner, and did not once wonder what to put next.

qa.q: What four boxes did Saurabh draw on each project page?
qa.a: He labelled the boxes problem, my part, result and link.

qa.q: What is Saurabh probably feeling on Saturday evening?
qa.a: Saurabh is probably satisfied and steady, since he finished two pages before dinner without wondering what came next.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Saurabh use if the design still feels vague, and why?
qa.a: Saurabh could copy the structure of one portfolio he likes and change the content, because a structure that already works removes guessing about layout.

qa.q: How does Gurleen see the sketches?
qa.a: Gurleen looks closely and circles the empty result box, so Gurleen sees the plan as useful and points out the missing piece before any code exists.

grounding: Shows sketching a portfolio site on paper and deciding what each project page must contain before coding.

passage: Leela, you asked why my portfolio still doesn't exist, so let me, Kunal, be honest. The first week I picked the font. The second week I changed the font. Then I decided the site needed a slide-in animation, and then a different one, and by the end of month one I had redesigned the top banner six times. I told myself it was not ready. Two months went by like that. Meanwhile, three of my classmates had put up plain pages and got interview calls. No one has seen my projects, not one recruiter, because there is nothing to click. I was so afraid of it being ordinary that I made it invisible. I still have not published it.

qa.q: How many times had Kunal redesigned the top banner?
qa.a: Kunal had redesigned the top banner six times.

qa.q: What was Kunal afraid of, according to the account?
qa.a: Kunal was afraid of the portfolio being ordinary, so it stayed hidden and nobody could see it.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Kunal use, and why?
qa.a: Kunal could publish a plain version this week and improve it later, because a visible page can get feedback and calls while an unpublished one cannot.

qa.q: How might Leela see Kunal's situation?
qa.a: Leela asked why the portfolio does not exist, and gets an honest answer, so Leela may see a friend whose skill is fine but who is stuck on polish.

grounding: Shows perfectionism about fonts and animations delaying a portfolio launch for months so that no recruiter ever sees the work.

subtype: Approach: minimum viable portfolio then iterate [Action]
passage:
"Do not write anything clever," said Hemant. "Just publish."
"But it's not finished," said Maria.
"It's a weekend. One page. Your name, two projects, one link each. That's all."
"And the fonts?"
"Default. Please."
On Sunday evening Maria sent the link. "It's live," she typed to her mentors, and her hands shook slightly. By Tuesday one had replied: "Add what the project actually does in one sentence." Another: "Good start, put your email at the top."
"See?" Hemant grinned. "You would have never got those if you had waited."
Maria opened the file. "One change a month. That's my rule now."

qa.q: What did Maria send on Sunday evening?
qa.a: Maria sent the link to her mentors.

qa.q: What is Maria feeling as she sends the link?
qa.a: Maria feels nervous and exposed, since her hands shook slightly, but she does it anyway.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Maria use to grow the site, and why?
qa.a: Maria could ask one mentor to review each change before the next month, because steady feedback shows which improvements actually matter.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Maria's hesitation?
qa.a: Hemant sees perfection as the obstacle and pushes for a plain page now, then grins when replies arrive, so Hemant treats early feedback as the prize.

grounding: Shows publishing a simple portfolio quickly, sharing it for feedback, and improving it in small monthly steps.

subtype: Approach: padding with copied tutorial projects [Pitfall]
passage:
Santosh: interview went badly
Tarun: what happened?
Santosh: he opened my portfolio. To-do app, weather app, calculator. Asked why I chose a database for the to-do app
Tarun: and?
Santosh: I froze. I followed a video for it. I couldn't say why
Santosh: he asked about the calculator too. Same. I copied every one
Tarun: ouch
Santosh: he said politely "thank you for showing your work" but I saw his face change. I think he stopped trusting the rest of my list
Tarun: what will you do?
Santosh: build one thing I can explain line by line. Not another clone

qa.q: Which three apps were in Santosh's portfolio?
qa.a: There were a to-do app, a weather app and a calculator.

qa.q: What is Santosh feeling after the interview?
qa.a: Santosh feels embarrassed and shaken, describing freezing when asked why, and worries that the interviewer stopped trusting the list.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Santosh use to build the portfolio, and why?
qa.a: Santosh could build one project around a real need and keep notes on each choice, because being able to explain decisions matters more than the number of apps.

qa.q: How might the interviewer have seen the portfolio?
qa.a: The interviewer saw three familiar apps and could not learn how Santosh thinks, so trust in the rest of the list dropped after the questions.

grounding: Shows padding a portfolio with copied tutorial projects and being unable to defend the choices in an interview.

subtype: Approach: solving a real local problem [Thinking]
passage: Noor, you asked why my portfolio has a shop sheet in it instead of another clone, so listen, I'm Abhinav. I was about to build my fifth tutorial app when I walked past Sharma Stores, the family shop near my hostel. The owner keeps stock in a notebook and runs out of things without noticing. I offered to build something. He said, "As long as it's simple." That word, simple, shaped everything. He does not use a laptop, only a phone. So I built a small sheet with three columns and a colour that turns red when stock is low. I sat there while he tried it and he got confused by one button, which I changed the same day. Now I have a story to tell an interviewer, and a real person who uses it.

qa.q: Where did Abhinav notice the stock problem?
qa.a: Abhinav noticed it at Sharma Stores, the family shop near the hostel.

qa.q: What did Abhinav feel when the shop owner got confused by a button?
qa.a: Abhinav felt alert and responsive, changing the button the same day because a real person's confusion counted.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Abhinav add, and why?
qa.a: Abhinav could count how many stock-outs happen before and after the sheet, because a small number would turn the story into evidence for interviewers.

qa.q: How might the shop owner see Abhinav's sheet?
qa.a: The owner asked for something simple, used the sheet on a phone and got confused once, so the owner sees a helpful student who listens.

grounding: Shows choosing a small real problem for a nearby shop instead of a clone, gaining a user, limits and a story for the portfolio.

subtype: Approach: asking peers and seniors to critique it [Revision]
passage: Aditi, let old Nitin tell you about my first portfolio. I was so proud of it. Each project had a line: "Built with React, Node and MongoDB." Tools, tools, tools. A senior, Suresh Bhai, looked at it over tea and said, "Nitin, I know what you used. What happened because of it?" I had no answer. He said, "Tell me the problem, what you built, and what got better." I was quiet, then a little annoyed, and then I went home and rewrote everything. The hostel mess project became: "Students queued 20 minutes for tokens; I built a tap-to-order page; queue dropped to five." Suresh Bhai read it again and just nodded. That nod was worth ten compliments.

qa.q: What did Suresh Bhai ask about the tools?
qa.a: Suresh Bhai asked what happened because of them.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling right after the senior's question?
qa.a: Nitin was quiet and a little annoyed at first, because there was no answer to the question.

qa.q: What choice inside the story turned the portfolio around, and why?
qa.a: Nitin rewrote each project around the problem, what was built and what got better, because outcomes showed value where a list of tools did not.

qa.q: How did Suresh Bhai see the first version of the portfolio?
qa.a: Suresh Bhai saw a long list of tools with no results, so he asked a plain question and nodded at the rewrite.

grounding: Shows getting critique from a senior, noticing that descriptions lack outcomes, and rewriting them around problem, work and result.

passage: Sunday morning in the hostel common room, Darshan set out a large mug of tea, his laptop and a folder of screenshots, and told his friend Karthik, "Today I do all the write-ups. All of them." "All six?" "All six. One sitting." In the earlier weeks, he had written a paragraph here, a paragraph there between assignments, and each time had to remember what the project did. This time he opened all the projects in a row, took the screenshots, wrote three lines about each, and named each file the same way. Karthik brought samosas at noon. By four o'clock the six summaries were done, and the page looked like a single piece of work instead of six.

qa.q: How many project write-ups did Darshan plan to finish that Sunday?
qa.a: Darshan planned to finish all six write-ups.

qa.q: How does Darshan feel by four o'clock?
qa.a: Darshan seems satisfied and relieved, since the six summaries are done and the page looks whole.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Darshan use for future projects, and why?
qa.a: Darshan could write a short note and take a screenshot as each project ends, because a small habit stops a big backlog from building up.

qa.q: How does Karthik see Darshan's Sunday plan?
qa.a: Karthik double-checks that all six will be done and brings samosas at noon, so Karthik supports the effort with company and food.

grounding: Shows setting aside one Sunday to write every project summary and capture screenshots in one sitting, which is quicker than fitting them between assignments.

subtype: Approach: comparing with others and feeling behind [Pitfall]
passage: Nilesh, sit down, let old Sabina tell you something. When I finished my first portfolio I was proud for exactly one day. Then I scrolled through pages from the big technical institutes. Sleek animations, dark themes, projects with hundreds of users. I looked at mine and thought, "Nobody would want to see this." I closed the tab. For four months I told nobody it existed. Meanwhile a friend who had been on the same course got an internship with a much plainer page. When she finally saw mine, she said, "This is good. Why is it hiding?" I had no answer. The work was decent. I had only compared it with the wrong people, and the cost was four months of doors I never knocked on.

qa.q: How many months did Sabina keep the portfolio secret?
qa.a: Sabina kept it secret for four months.

qa.q: What was Sabina feeling when she compared her pages with the institutes' pages?
qa.a: Sabina felt small and discouraged, deciding that nobody would want to see the page and closing the tab.

qa.q: What choice inside the story could Sabina have made at that moment, and why?
qa.a: Sabina could have shown the page to a friend or mentor, because an outside view might have shown it was decent before doubt turned into delay.

qa.q: How did Sabina's friend see the portfolio?
qa.a: The friend, who had got an internship with a plainer page, called it good and asked why it was hiding, so the friend saw the work more kindly than Sabina did.

grounding: Shows comparing one's portfolio with very polished ones, feeling behind, and delaying sharing even though the work was decent.

subtype: Approach: tracking which pieces get attention [Revision]
passage: Jagdish, you asked how I improved the portfolio, and the honest answer is: I watched. I'm Sachin, and for two weeks I checked which projects people actually opened, since the site kept a simple count. Twelve visits went to the chess timer that had a live link. Two went to the report analyser. The recruiter emails I got mentioned the timer every time. So I moved it to the very first spot on the page, above everything else. And I noticed the pattern, so I spent a weekend putting one more project online with a link that works. Now two of my projects can be tried by anyone. The count of visits tripled, and one recruiter wrote, "I clicked the link and it worked."

qa.q: How many visits went to the chess timer?
qa.a: Twelve visits went to the chess timer.

qa.q: What did Sachin feel when noticing which project people opened?
qa.a: Sachin felt curious and motivated, seeing a clear pattern that pointed to what to do next.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Sachin add to learn more, and why?
qa.a: Sachin could ask two recruiters what they looked at first, because visit counts show clicks but not the reasons behind them.

qa.q: How might a recruiter see the live link?
qa.a: A recruiter can try the project at once and see it work, which builds trust faster than reading a description.

grounding: Shows watching which portfolio pieces get attention and reorganising around the deployed project.
